title: The Letter to the Romans
summary: Paul’s longest letter, written to the believers in Rome before he had met them: an argument about how a person is put right with God, by faith and not by keeping the law, what that means for Jews and Gentiles alike, and how believers should then live. 16 chapters.

primer.a: 这不是故事，是一封信。写信的人叫保罗，是最早把对耶稣的信仰传到各地的人之一（他的经历见《使徒行传》后半卷）；收信的是罗马城里信耶稣的人，保罗当时还没去过那里。一般认为这封信写在公元 57 年前后，用的是当时通行的希腊文。新约里保罗的信有十几封，这一封最长，也排在最前面。
从头到尾是保罗一个人在说话，所以本站的译文整封信不加引号。「我」是保罗，「你们」是罗马的信徒。他常常自己提一个问题再自己回答（「那么我们要说什么呢？」「绝对不是！」），像在和一个看不见的人辩论；这时候的「你」不是指收信的人，而是他设想出来的反对者。引号只用在他引旧约的话、或替别人说出一句话的地方。
最早信耶稣的人全是犹太人，照旧守犹太人的律法。后来不是犹太人的外族人也来信了，于是有了争论：外族人要不要先照犹太人的规矩受割礼、守律法；犹太人和外族人在上帝面前是不是一样。罗马的信徒里两种人都有。保罗打算去罗马，再从那里去更西边的西班牙，写这封信是先向他们说明自己传的是什么。

primer.q: 读的时候会卡住的地方
primer.a: 一是它在讲道理，不在讲故事：一句接一句地推论，「因为」「所以」「那么」特别多，一节常常只是半句话。读不下去时先看每章开头的导读，知道这一章要论证什么再读。二是几个字反复出现而且意思很重：义、信、恩典、律法、罪、肉体、灵。这些词每章第一次出现时括号里有一句说明，但括号说不尽，同一个词在不同地方轻重也不同。三是大段引旧约，有时一连引好几处。四是有几段历来争论很大（第 1 章后半、第 9–11 章讲以色列、第 13 章讲掌权的人），本站照原文译，不缓和、不加强，也不加评论。五是最后一章几乎全是问安的人名，可以跳过。
这些词在信里反复出现，先认一下。括号里的说明只是最短的通行解释。
terms: 义、称义
「义」是在上帝面前算为对。「称义」是被上帝算为对、被他接纳。这封信的中心问题就是：人凭什么被称为义。
信
信靠。信里说人被称为义是凭着信，不是凭着守律法。
恩典
上帝白白给的好意，不是人挣来的。
律法
上帝通过摩西颁给犹太人的规矩。信里有几处这个词的意思是「规律、原则」，那时本站写「律」。
罪
违背上帝的事。信里常把它说成一股辖制人的势力，像一个主人。
肉体
在这封信里多半不是指身体，而是指人靠自己、不顺从上帝的那一面。
灵、圣灵
上帝的灵。信里把「顺着肉体活」和「顺着灵活」对着说。
外族人
不是犹太人的人。信里有时说「希腊人」，也是这个意思。
割礼
割去包皮的仪式，是犹太人身份的记号。
基督
希腊话，意思是「受膏的人」，就是上帝选立的那一位救主。在这封信里已经是耶稣的称号，常说「在基督里」。

primer.a: 全信 16 章，大致分四段：第 1–8 章讲人怎样在上帝面前被称为义，以及被称为义之后怎样活；第 9–11 章讲犹太人这个民族在这件事里的位置；第 12–15 章讲信的人日常该怎样彼此相待、怎样对待别人；第 16 章是问安。想先读好懂的，从第 12 章读起；想读最有名的一段，读第 8 章。头几章最难，不必强求一遍读懂。

primerEn.q: What kind of book this is
primerEn.a: This is not a story but a letter. Its writer, Paul, was one of the first to carry faith in Jesus from place to place (his story is told in the second half of Acts); its readers were the believers in Jesus in the city of Rome, which Paul had not yet visited. It is generally dated to about 57 CE and was written in the common Greek of the time. The New Testament has more than a dozen letters of Paul; this is the longest and stands first.

Paul speaks from beginning to end, so this site’s translation puts no quotation marks around the letter. "I" is Paul; "you" (plural) are the believers in Rome. He often asks a question and answers it himself ("What then shall we say?" "By no means!"), as if arguing with someone unseen; the "you" (singular) in those places is not the readers but an objector he imagines. Quotation marks appear only where he quotes the Old Testament or puts words in someone’s mouth.

The first believers in Jesus were all Jews and went on keeping the Jewish law. Then non-Jews came to believe too, and a dispute arose: must Gentiles first be circumcised and keep the law as Jews do, and do Jews and Gentiles stand alike before God? The believers in Rome included both. Paul planned to come to Rome and go on from there to Spain, farther west; he wrote this letter to set out in advance what it is he preaches.

First, it argues rather than narrates: one inference after another, full of "for," "therefore" and "then," and a verse is often only half a sentence. If you lose the thread, read the introduction at the head of each chapter to see what it is trying to show. Second, a few words recur and carry great weight: righteousness, faith, grace, law, sin, flesh, Spirit. Third, the Old Testament is quoted at length, sometimes several passages in a row. Fourth, some passages have long been fiercely disputed (the second half of chapter 1, chapters 9–11 on Israel, chapter 13 on the authorities); this site translates them as they stand, neither softened nor sharpened, and without comment. Fifth, the last chapter is almost all greetings to named people and can be skipped.
These words recur throughout the letter. The glosses are only the shortest common explanations.
terms: Righteousness, to justify
"Righteousness" is being in the right before God. "To be justified" is to be counted right and accepted by him. The letter’s central question is on what basis a person is justified.
Faith
Trust. The letter says a person is justified by faith, not by keeping the law.
Grace
God’s freely given favor, not something earned.
The law
The rules God gave the Jews through Moses. In a few places the word means "principle" or "rule" instead.
Sin
What goes against God. The letter often speaks of it as a power that rules people, like a master.
Flesh
In this letter usually not the body but the side of a person that relies on itself and does not submit to God.
Spirit
The Spirit of God. The letter sets "living according to the flesh" against "living according to the Spirit."
Gentiles
People who are not Jews. The letter sometimes says "Greeks" in the same sense.
Circumcision
The cutting away of the foreskin, the mark of being a Jew.
Christ
Greek for "anointed one," the deliverer chosen by God. In this letter it is already a title for Jesus, often in the phrase "in Christ."

primerEn.a: The letter has 16 chapters in roughly four parts: chapters 1–8, how a person is justified before God and how to live once justified; chapters 9–11, the place of the Jewish people in all this; chapters 12–15, how believers should treat one another and others day to day; chapter 16, greetings. For the easiest way in, start at chapter 12; for the best-known passage, read chapter 8. The opening chapters are the hardest, and there is no need to grasp them in one reading.

compare: 希腊文原文用 SBL Greek New Testament（SBLGNT），只去掉了底本里的校勘符号，经文本身没有动；罗马转写是本站按通行规则机械生成的，不标重音。

白话是写给完全没接触过圣经的人看的：用平常说话的词，长句拆短，但一节对一节，原文有的意思不少、原文没有的不添。原文没有、但不补就看不懂的字，一律放在圆括号（）里；括号里是通行的解释，不是经文本身。这封信里抽象的说法很多（「上帝的义」「信的顺从」「罪的律」），白话照原文的结构译，没有把它们改写成一句解释；有两种通行读法的地方，正文取一种，另一种写在那一节下面。英文版贴着字面译，不加括号。白话、英文和所有说明都是 AI 从希腊文译写的，没有经过圣经学者或教会审阅。
对照栏是 1919 年出版的官话和合译本（和合本），录文取自维基文库，繁体转成简体，几个异体字改成了通行写法，原书的旧式标点照录。维基文库录的是称「神」的版本；本站的白话写「上帝」。人名跟和合本走；和合本的「外邦人」本站写「外族人」。

这封信的结尾，本站依据的希腊文底本和和合本排得不一样。底本的第 16 章到第 24 节结束，第 24 节是一句祝福；和合本没有这句祝福，它把第 23 节的问安拆成第 23、24 两节，后面第 25–27 节是一段颂词，底本没有收。本站节号跟底本：第 23 节的对照栏放了和合本的两节，第 24 节的对照栏是空的，第 25–27 节留着节号、原文栏放一个「—」，对照栏照录和合本的颂词。这段颂词在各种古抄本里位置不一，有的在这里，有的在第 14 章末，有的没有。
这是一封信，全篇是保罗一个人在说话，所以译文整篇不加引号。他设想别人反问的地方、引旧约的地方才用引号。信里引旧约，白话照这封信的希腊文译，和旧约原处的字句常有出入，出处写在对照注里。
compareEn: The Greek is the SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) with its text-critical sigla removed and nothing else changed; the romanization is generated mechanically by this site under the usual conventions, without accents.

The Chinese is written for readers who have never opened a Bible: everyday words and shorter sentences, but verse for verse, with nothing in the Greek left out and nothing added. Words that are not in the Greek but are needed to follow it are put in parentheses; they give the usual explanation and are not part of the text. The letter is full of abstract phrases ("the righteousness of God," "the obedience of faith," "the law of sin"); the Chinese keeps their structure rather than rewriting them as explanations, and where there are two common readings it follows one in the text and gives the other under that verse. The English stays close to the wording and adds no parentheses. The Chinese, the English and all the notes were translated and written by AI from the Greek and have not been reviewed by biblical scholars or by any church.

The older Chinese version shown alongside is the Mandarin Union Version of 1919, taken from Chinese Wikisource, converted to simplified characters with a few variant characters normalized and its original punctuation kept. Wikisource carries the edition that calls God 神 (Shén); this site’s plain Chinese writes 上帝 (Shàngdì). Names follow the Union Version.

At the end of the letter the Greek edition this site follows and the Union Version are arranged differently. The edition’s chapter 16 ends at verse 24, a blessing. The Union Version lacks that blessing; it splits the greetings of verse 23 into verses 23 and 24, and then has a doxology as verses 25–27, which the edition does not include. This site follows the edition’s numbering: both Union Version verses are shown beside verse 23, nothing beside verse 24, and verses 25–27 keep their numbers with a dash in the Greek column and the Union Version’s doxology alongside. In the ancient manuscripts this doxology stands in different places: here, at the end of chapter 14, or nowhere.

This is a letter, Paul speaking throughout, so the translation puts no quotation marks around it; they appear only where he imagines an objection or quotes the Old Testament. Those quotations are translated from this letter’s Greek, so the wording often differs from the Old Testament passage itself, whose reference is given in the notes.
